entries.title: Sauce tomate
entries.summary: The classical French tomato sauce: tomatoes cooked with salt pork, a mirepoix, garlic and white stock, then passed through a sieve until smooth. One of Escoffier's four base sauces, it is the parent of provençale and portugaise, and New Orleans' Creole sauce is its cousin.
entries.guest: Sauce tomate is the French kitchen's tomato sauce: ripe tomatoes slow cooked with a little pork, vegetables and stock, then sieved smooth. It is rounder and silkier than a quick tomato sauce.

paras: Sauce tomate is the French kitchen's tomato sauce, and one of the five mother sauces taught today. Tomatoes are cooked slowly with salt pork or bacon, a mirepoix (diced carrot and onion cooked in fat as a flavour base), garlic, herbs and white stock, then sieved so only a smooth, brick red sauce comes through. Most kitchens now thicken it by reduction alone, cooking it down until it coats a spoon, rather than with a roux.
It matters because so much grows from it, and in New Orleans its nearest cousin is the Creole sauce.

Render 50 g (2 oz) of diced salt pork or unsmoked bacon in a little butter over gentle heat until the fat runs. Add 75 g (2.5 oz) each of diced carrot and onion, a bay leaf and a sprig of thyme, and cook for 8 to 10 minutes until soft and lightly golden. For the classical version, stir in 30 g (1 oz) of flour and cook it for 2 minutes.

Add 2 kg (4.4 lb) of ripe tomatoes, roughly chopped, or the same weight of tinned plum tomatoes with their juice, then 500 ml (about 2 cups) of white stock, a crushed clove of garlic, salt, pepper and a pinch of sugar. Bring it to the boil, cover and cook in a low oven, about 160°C (320°F), or at the barest simmer on the stove, for 1.5 to 2 hours, stirring from the bottom now and then.

Pass it through a food mill or fine sieve, pressing the pulp through and leaving skins, seeds, pork and vegetables behind. Reduce it gently in a clean pan until it coats a spoon, taste for salt and acidity, and dot the surface with butter so no skin forms. It makes a little over 1 litre (about 1 quart).

The daughters are made by addition. Provençale brings garlic and olive oil, with parsley or other herbs. Portugaise softens chopped onion in oil, then adds garlic, chopped tomato flesh and parsley. In New Orleans the family has a cousin in the Creole sauce, built on the holy trinity of onion, celery and green pepper, with a logic of its own rather than a classical daughter's; at Brennan's it is the sauce on the New Orleans Shrimp & Grits.

An Italian sugo is a cousin, not a daughter: usually tomatoes, olive oil, garlic or onion and perhaps basil, cooked for a shorter time and often left with some texture. Sauce tomate has stock, pork and mirepoix behind it, cooks longer and is sieved smooth, so it tastes rounder and meatier.

Raw acidity, a sharp, thin taste, comes from underripe tomatoes or too short a cook: cook it longer and round it with a pinch of sugar or a piece of butter. A scorched base comes from tomato sugars catching on the pan: use a heavy pan and gentle heat, stir from the bottom, and if it catches, pour the sauce into a clean pan without scraping and taste it; a burnt note that runs through means starting again. A sauce too thin to coat needs more gentle reduction after sieving, never a spoonful of raw flour.

Carême's four great sauces, in the early nineteenth century, had no tomato among them; Escoffier counted sauce tomate among his four base sauces in Le Guide culinaire (1903). He fried diced salt pork with carrot and onion, stirred in a little flour as a light roux, added tomatoes, white stock and garlic, and cooked it covered in the oven before sieving it. Later cooks dropped the flour and let reduction do the work, for a brighter sauce.

Choose for ripeness. In their summer season, ripe Creole tomatoes, Louisiana's own, make a sweet, bright sauce. The rest of the year, good tinned plum tomatoes, picked and packed ripe, beat pale fresh ones; plum varieties carry more flesh and less water, so they cook down faster.

At the table, call it a smooth, slow-cooked tomato sauce, rounder than a quick marinara because it is cooked with stock and a little pork. Mention both to a guest who avoids pork or meat, and send every such question to the kitchen, because a house recipe may differ from the classical one.

cards.front: What is sauce tomate?
cards.back: The classical French tomato sauce: tomatoes cooked with salt pork, mirepoix, garlic and white stock, then passed through a sieve until smooth.

cards.front: What thickens a modern sauce tomate, where most mother sauces use a roux?
cards.back: Reduction: the tomato pulp is cooked down until it coats a spoon, so no starch is needed.

cards.front: How did Escoffier's sauce tomate differ from most made today?
cards.back: He stirred a little flour into the fat as a light roux; later cooks dropped it and let reduction thicken the sauce, for a brighter taste.

cards.front: What goes into the pan before the tomatoes?
cards.back: Salt pork or bacon rendered in butter, then diced carrot and onion with bay and thyme, cooked until soft and lightly golden for a sweet base.

cards.front: What is a working ratio of tomatoes to stock?
cards.back: About 2 kg (4.4 lb) of tomatoes to 500 ml (about 2 cups) of white stock, cooked 1.5 to 2 hours, then reduced to coat.

cards.front: How does sauce tomate differ from a simple Italian tomato sauce?
cards.back: It has stock, salt pork and a mirepoix behind it, cooks longer and is sieved smooth, so it tastes rounder and meatier.

cards.front: What does provençale add to sauce tomate?
cards.back: Garlic and olive oil, with parsley or other herbs: the southern, sunny daughter of the tomato family.

cards.front: What makes a sauce portugaise?
cards.back: Chopped onion softened in oil, then garlic, chopped tomato flesh and parsley, added to the tomato sauce for texture and sweetness.

cards.front: Which New Orleans sauce is a cousin of the tomato family, and where does Brennan's serve it?
cards.back: The Creole sauce, built on the holy trinity of onion, celery and green pepper rather than on stock and pork; at Brennan's it is on the New Orleans Shrimp & Grits.

cards.front: Which tomatoes should you choose for sauce tomate?
cards.back: Ripe Creole tomatoes in their summer season; the rest of the year, good tinned plum tomatoes, picked and packed ripe, beat pale fresh ones.

cards.front: A sauce tomate tastes sharp and raw. What went wrong, and what is the fix?
cards.back: Underripe tomatoes or too short a cook. Cook it longer, and round it with a pinch of sugar or a piece of butter.

cards.front: What do you do when a tomato sauce catches on the bottom of the pan?
cards.back: Pour it into a clean pan without scraping and taste it; if the burnt note runs through the sauce, start again.

questions.q: What thickens most modern versions of sauce tomate?
questions.answer: Reduction alone
questions.why: The pulp is cooked down until it coats a spoon; tomato carries enough body that no starch or yolk is needed.

questions.q: What did Escoffier's sauce tomate include that most modern versions leave out?
questions.answer: A little flour, as a light roux
distractors: Red wine reduced almost to a glaze
questions.why: Escoffier stirred flour into the fat before the tomatoes went in; later cooks let reduction alone thicken the sauce, which tastes brighter.

questions.q: Compared with a quick Italian tomato sauce, what sets sauce tomate apart?
questions.answer: Stock, salt pork and mirepoix, then sieving
distractors: Olive oil and basil, cooked briefly
Cream and Parmesan stirred in at the end
Vinegar and sugar cooked to a glaze
questions.why: Sauce tomate is built like a French mother, on pork, aromatics and stock, then cooked long and sieved smooth.

questions.q: Which daughter of sauce tomate is built on garlic, olive oil and herbs?
questions.answer: Provençale
questions.why: Provençale adds garlic and olive oil with herbs; portugaise leans on onion and tomato flesh, Mornay comes from béchamel and Bercy from velouté.

questions.q: Which New Orleans sauce is taught as a cousin of sauce tomate?
questions.answer: Creole sauce
questions.why: The Creole sauce cooks the holy trinity into tomatoes and stock, a cousin rather than a classical daughter; marchand de vin is brown, béarnaise an emulsion and beurre blanc a butter sauce.

questions.q: Out of season, which tomatoes make a better sauce tomate than pale fresh ones?
questions.answer: Good tinned plum tomatoes
questions.why: Tinned plum tomatoes are picked and packed ripe, with more flesh and less water, so they cook down sweeter than pale winter fruit.

questions.q: A sauce tomate tastes sharp and raw. What is the likeliest cause?
questions.answer: Underripe fruit or a short cook
distractors: Too long, covered, in a low oven
questions.why: Acid mellows as tomatoes cook and ripe fruit brings sugar; cook longer and round the sauce with a pinch of sugar or butter.

questions.q: A tomato sauce has caught on the bottom of the pan. What should you do first?
questions.answer: Decant it without scraping
distractors: Stir the burnt layer in for colour
Add sugar to hide the taste
Turn up the heat to finish faster
questions.why: Scraping spreads the burnt taste through the sauce; move what is clean, taste it, and start again if the bitterness has spread.

entries.title: Hollandaise
entries.summary: A warm emulsion of egg yolk and butter, sharpened with lemon juice or a vinegar reduction. It is the one mother sauce bound by egg yolk: quick to make, fragile in service and the parent of a whole family.
entries.guest: Hollandaise is a warm butter sauce thickened with egg yolk and brightened with lemon. On the Eggs Hussarde it shares the plate with a red wine sauce.

paras: Hollandaise is a warm emulsion: tiny droplets of butterfat held apart in a little water by egg yolk, whose proteins and lecithin, a natural emulsifier, coat each droplet so it cannot join the next. Acid, either lemon juice or a reduction of vinegar and peppercorns, sharpens the flavour and helps the yolk stay smooth under heat. It is the one mother sauce thickened by yolk rather than by roux or reduction, which makes it quick, fragile and unforgiving of carelessness.
For a new cook it is the sauce that teaches heat control; for a server, the sauce guests know from Eggs Benedict and the door into a large family, béarnaise first.

Allow about one yolk for every 60 to 85 g (2 to 3 oz) of butter. A dependable batch is 3 yolks to 225 g (8 oz) of clarified butter, about 75 g a yolk, with 30 ml (2 tbsp) of reduction or lemon juice, a spoonful of water, salt and a pinch of cayenne. One yolk can hold far more fat, but a sauce pushed to its limit breaks at the first knock, so the ratio buys a margin for service.
Clarified butter, with its water and milk solids removed, gives a firmer, steadier hollandaise; whole melted butter brings its own water and gives a lighter, looser sauce with a milkier taste.

Reduce white wine vinegar with crushed white peppercorns and a little water, strain it and let it cool. Whisk the yolks with the reduction in a bowl set over barely simmering water, never touching it, until they foam and then thicken into a pale ribbon that holds its shape for a moment. That happens at about 60 to 65°C (140 to 149°F). Past about 70°C (158°F) the yolk proteins begin to set into curds, so lift the bowl away whenever the edges thicken too fast.

Off the heat, whisk in the warm butter a few drops at a time until the sauce takes, then in a thin, steady stream. Season with salt, a squeeze of lemon and a pinch of cayenne. If it stiffens, loosen it with a few drops of warm water.

Read the finished sauce by eye and spoon. It should coat the spoon thickly enough to hold a line drawn through it with a finger, look glossy rather than dull or oily, be pale yellow, and feel warm, never hot: around 60°C (140°F). Keeping it there through a long service is its own lesson, in the entry on holding warm emulsions.

A hollandaise fails in two directions. Too hot, and the yolk scrambles into a grainy, curdled sauce. Butter added too fast, a base gone too cool, or a sauce pushed too thick with too little water, and the fat escapes, leaving a greasy, split pool. The quick fix for a split is to whisk the broken sauce, drop by drop, into a spoonful of warm water or a fresh yolk in a clean bowl. The full set of rescues belongs to the entry on breaking and rescuing.

The name means Dutch sauce, though no clear link to Holland has been found. Modern kitchens teach hollandaise as the fifth mother sauce. Carême's four great sauces did not include it, and Escoffier's French Le Guide culinaire (1903) named four base sauces and placed hollandaise among the smaller sauces. The English translation of 1907, A Guide to Modern Cookery, prints it in its chapter of leading warm sauces, and later schools made five the standard lesson. It earns its place as a mother through its large family.

On the floor, describe hollandaise as a warm butter sauce thickened with egg yolk and brightened with lemon, the sauce guests know from Eggs Benedict. Its yolks are only lightly cooked, so any question about eggs, butter or how the sauce is made goes to the kitchen, never to a guess.

At Brennan's, hollandaise is the rich, lemony layer on the Eggs Hussarde and the Eggs Owen. Each pairs it with marchand de vin, a dark red wine sauce beneath the egg, so the plate carries one bright sauce and one deep one. Describe it as the classic Benedict sauce, and send any question about what goes into it to the kitchen.

brennans.how: Hollandaise goes over the poached eggs and coffee-cured Canadian bacon, with marchand de vin beneath, so the plate carries a bright sauce over a deep one.
Over the soft-boiled egg, the red-wine-braised short rib débris and the Creole-spiced potato, hollandaise brings butter and lemon against the marchand de vin.

cards.front: What kind of sauce is hollandaise?
cards.back: A warm emulsion of egg yolk and butter, sharpened with lemon juice or a vinegar reduction.

cards.front: What thickens hollandaise, where most mother sauces use a roux?
cards.back: Egg yolk: its proteins and lecithin hold droplets of butterfat apart in a little water, so no flour is needed.

cards.front: What is a dependable ratio of yolks to butter?
cards.back: About one yolk to 60 to 85 g (2 to 3 oz) of butter; a working batch is 3 yolks to 225 g (8 oz), which leaves a margin for service.

cards.front: How do you know the yolks are ready for the butter?
cards.back: They thicken into a pale ribbon that holds its shape for a moment, at about 60 to 65°C (140 to 149°F).

cards.front: What happens when the yolk base gets too hot?
cards.back: The yolk proteins set into curds and the sauce turns grainy; past about 70°C (158°F) the risk climbs fast.

cards.front: What splits a hollandaise, and what is the quick fix?
cards.back: Butter added too fast, or a sauce too cool or too thick. Whisk the broken sauce drop by drop into warm water or a fresh yolk in a clean bowl.

cards.front: Why do many cooks make hollandaise with clarified butter?
cards.back: Clarified butter has had its water and milk solids taken out, so it gives a firmer, steadier sauce; whole melted butter gives a lighter, looser one.

cards.front: How warm should a finished hollandaise be?
cards.back: Warm, never hot: around 60°C (140°F), off direct heat. Hotter and the yolk scrambles; cooler and the sauce stiffens and can split.

cards.front: What does a finished hollandaise look like?
cards.back: Thick enough to coat a spoon and hold a line drawn through it, glossy rather than oily, pale yellow and warm.

cards.front: Did Escoffier's French Guide culinaire (1903) count hollandaise among its base sauces?
cards.back: No: the French book named four base sauces and set hollandaise among the smaller sauces. The 1907 English translation prints it among the leading warm sauces, and the five came with later teaching.

cards.front: Name three sauces built on hollandaise.
cards.back: Béarnaise, with its tarragon reduction; mousseline, with whipped cream folded in; and maltaise, with blood orange.

cards.front: Which Brennan's dishes carry hollandaise?
cards.back: The Eggs Hussarde and the Eggs Owen, each with marchand de vin, a red wine sauce, alongside it.

questions.q: What holds a hollandaise together, where most mother sauces rely on a roux?
questions.answer: Egg yolk
questions.why: The yolk's proteins and lecithin keep droplets of butterfat dispersed in water, so hollandaise needs no starch at all.

questions.q: Which proportion is a dependable working ratio for hollandaise?
questions.answer: 3 yolks to 225 g (8 oz) of clarified butter
distractors: 1 yolk to 500 g (1 lb) of clarified butter
6 yolks to 50 g (2 oz) of clarified butter
3 yolks to 1 litre (about 1 quart) of warm milk
questions.why: That is about 75 g a yolk, inside the working range of 60 to 85 g; one yolk can take more, but with no margin.

questions.q: At roughly what temperature are the yolks ready to take the butter?
questions.why: The yolks thicken to a ribbon in that window; cooler and they stay thin, and past about 70°C (158°F) their proteins set into curds.

questions.q: A hollandaise has split into a greasy pool. What is the classic rescue?
questions.answer: Whisk it slowly into warm water or a yolk
distractors: Boil it hard until it comes back together
Whisk in a spoonful of flour over high heat
Chill it, then beat in cold butter
questions.why: A fresh base gives the fat something to disperse into, and adding the broken sauce slowly rebuilds the emulsion a droplet at a time.

questions.q: How warm should a hollandaise be when it goes onto the plate?
questions.answer: Warm, around 60°C (140°F), never hot
distractors: Piping hot, straight from direct heat
Fridge cold, so it sets firm
Room temperature, after an hour's rest
questions.why: Hotter and the yolk scrambles, cooler and the sauce stiffens and splits; warm and off direct heat keeps it smooth and glossy.

questions.q: Which of these sauces is a daughter of hollandaise?
questions.answer: Béarnaise
questions.why: Béarnaise is hollandaise built on a vinegar, shallot and tarragon reduction; Mornay and Soubise come from béchamel, and bordelaise from the brown sauces.

questions.q: On which Brennan's dish does hollandaise share the plate with marchand de vin?
questions.answer: Eggs Hussarde
questions.why: The Eggs Hussarde, like the Eggs Owen, carries hollandaise with marchand de vin; the Sardou carries Choron, the hanger steak béarnaise and the Chateaubriand Foyot.

questions.q: Why does clarified butter give a firmer hollandaise than whole butter?
questions.answer: Its water and milk solids are gone
distractors: It is whipped full of air first
It has been browned to a nutty colour
questions.why: Whole butter brings its own water, which loosens the sauce; clarified butter is almost pure fat, so the same yolks set a firmer emulsion.

questions.q: Which describes a finished hollandaise that is ready to serve?
questions.answer: Glossy, pale and holding a line
distractors: Grainy, with small curds through it
Thin enough to run like milk
Oily, with butter pooling at the edge
questions.why: Gloss and a line that holds show a sound emulsion; curds mean too much heat and pooling butter means the sauce has split.

questions.q: A hollandaise base gets too hot before the butter goes in. What happens to it?
questions.answer: The yolks set into curds
distractors: It thickens into a smooth ribbon
questions.why: Past about 70°C (158°F) the yolk proteins set and the sauce turns grainy, so the bowl is lifted off the heat whenever the edges thicken too fast.

entries.title: Béarnaise
entries.summary: Hollandaise built on a sharp reduction of white wine, tarragon vinegar, shallot and tarragon, and finished with fresh herbs. Firmer and sharper than its parent, it is the classic sauce for grilled beef and the base of Choron and Foyot.
entries.guest: Béarnaise is a warm butter and egg yolk sauce sharpened with tarragon and shallot. It is the classic French sauce for steak, and it comes with our breakfast hanger steak.

paras: Béarnaise is hollandaise's best-known daughter: a warm emulsion of egg yolk and butter, built on its own sharp reduction. White wine, tarragon vinegar, chopped shallot, tarragon stalks, chervil and crushed peppercorns are boiled down until almost dry, and that concentrate flavours the whole sauce. Tarragon is a herb with a clear aniseed note; chervil is a soft herb, milder and sweeter. Both go in again, fresh and chopped, at the end.
The acid and the herbs give béarnaise a sharper, greener taste and a firmer body than hollandaise, which is why it stands up to grilled and roast beef.

For 3 yolks and 225 g (8 oz) of clarified or melted butter, put 60 ml (1/4 cup) of tarragon or white wine vinegar and 60 ml (1/4 cup) of dry white wine in a small pan with two finely chopped shallots, a few tarragon stalks, a sprig of chervil and a pinch of crushed peppercorns. Reduce until only about 30 ml (2 tbsp) of liquid is left, almost dry. The reduction should taste fiercely sharp on its own, because the butter will soften it a great deal.

Let the reduction cool a little, then strain it for a smooth sauce, or leave the shallot in for texture; both are seen in good kitchens. Whisk it with the yolks over barely simmering water until they thicken to a ribbon, at about 60 to 65°C (140 to 149°F), then take the bowl off the heat and mount the warm butter in, slowly at first. To mount is to whisk fat into a sauce so that it thickens and shines.
Béarnaise is usually made a little thicker than hollandaise, so it sits on hot meat instead of running off it. Finish with chopped tarragon and chervil, taste for salt, and keep it warm, never hot.
Béarnaise breaks for the same reasons as hollandaise, overheated yolks or butter added too fast, and it mends the same way: whisk it drop by drop into a little warm water or a fresh yolk.

Three faults are its own. A reduction left too wet carries too much water into the yolks, and the sauce comes out thin and slack; next time boil it down further, and for now whisk the thin sauce into a fresh yolk over gentle heat. A reduction too heavy on vinegar makes the sauce harsh; soften it with a little more butter. A sauce that tastes flat had a timid reduction: a few drops of vinegar and more fresh tarragon bring it back. Dried tarragon cannot stand in at the finish.

Tradition credits the sauce to the chef Collinet at the Pavillon Henri IV in Saint-Germain-en-Laye, west of Paris, around 1836, and says he named it for Béarn, the region of south-west France where Henri IV was born. The date and even the chef's name vary between accounts, so tell it as tradition. Its place in the classical repertoire is not in doubt: it is the best-known daughter of hollandaise.

Béarnaise has children of its own. Choron folds in tomato cooked down to a paste, which turns the sauce a soft coral without thinning it. Foyot, which many texts also call Valois, whisks in glace de viande, a reduced meat glaze, for a tawny, deeper sauce. Foyot keeps the fresh tarragon; Escoffier's Choron leaves out the final chopped tarragon and chervil, though many kitchens keep them. Both have their own entry.

At Brennan's, béarnaise is printed on the breakfast Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak as French béarnaise, beside a sunny-side-up egg and a smoked potato pavé, a neat, layered block of potato. Its daughters work elsewhere on the menu: Choron replaces the usual hollandaise on the Eggs Sardou, and Foyot brings depth to the Roasted Chateaubriand, a lean cut given a rich sauce.

To a guest, béarnaise is a warm butter and egg yolk sauce sharpened with shallot and tarragon, the classic French sauce for steak. A guest who knows hollandaise can hear it as hollandaise's sharper, herbal daughter. Any question about eggs, butter or how it is made goes to the kitchen.

The Eggs Sardou carries Choron, béarnaise with tomato, over poached eggs, crispy artichokes and Parmesan creamed spinach.
The Roasted Chateaubriand for two comes with sauce Foyot, béarnaise deepened with meat glaze, to give the lean tenderloin richness.

cards.front: What is béarnaise, in one line?
cards.back: Hollandaise built on a reduction of white wine, tarragon vinegar, shallot and tarragon, finished with fresh tarragon and chervil.

cards.front: What goes into a béarnaise reduction?
cards.back: White wine, tarragon or white wine vinegar, chopped shallot, tarragon stalks, chervil and crushed peppercorns, reduced almost dry, to about 30 ml (2 tbsp).

cards.front: Which fresh herbs finish a béarnaise?
cards.back: Chopped tarragon, the defining flavour, and chervil, added at the end so they stay green and bright.

cards.front: How should béarnaise differ in body from hollandaise?
cards.back: It is usually made a little thicker, so it sits on hot meat instead of running off it.

cards.front: Is the shallot strained out of the reduction or left in?
cards.back: Either: strain it for a smooth sauce, or leave the shallot in for texture. Both are seen in good kitchens.

cards.front: Where and when is béarnaise usually said to have been created?
cards.back: At the Pavillon Henri IV in Saint-Germain-en-Laye around 1836, credited to the chef Collinet, though accounts differ, so it is told as tradition.

cards.front: Where does béarnaise take its name from?
cards.back: From Béarn, the region of south-west France where Henri IV was born.

cards.front: How does a finished béarnaise become Choron or Foyot?
cards.back: One addition, off the heat: Choron folds in tomato cooked down to a thick paste, and Foyot whisks in warm glace de viande, a reduced meat glaze. Each has its own entry.

cards.front: What is béarnaise classically served with, and why does it suit it?
cards.back: Grilled and roast beef, steak above all: its vinegar and tarragon cut through the richness of the meat. Hollandaise leans more to eggs, fish and vegetables.

cards.front: Which Brennan's dishes carry béarnaise or its daughters?
cards.back: The breakfast hanger steak carries béarnaise, the Eggs Sardou carries Choron and the Roasted Chateaubriand carries Foyot.

cards.front: How do you lift a béarnaise that tastes flat?
cards.back: Add a few drops of vinegar and more fresh tarragon; a flat sauce usually had a timid reduction.

cards.front: What happens when a béarnaise reduction is left too wet?
cards.back: It carries too much water into the yolks and the sauce comes out thin and slack; reduce until about 30 ml (2 tbsp) is left.

questions.q: Which herb gives béarnaise its defining flavour?
questions.answer: Tarragon
questions.why: Tarragon goes into the reduction and again, fresh, at the finish; its anise note is what sets béarnaise apart from hollandaise.

questions.q: What is reduced to begin a béarnaise?
questions.answer: Vinegar, white wine, shallot and tarragon
distractors: Red wine, shallot and bone marrow
Milk, onion, clove and a grating of nutmeg
questions.why: The sharp vinegar and herb reduction is the whole difference between béarnaise and hollandaise; red wine and marrow belong to bordelaise.

questions.q: To turn béarnaise into Choron or Foyot, when does the addition go in?
questions.answer: Into the finished sauce, off the heat
distractors: Into the reduction, before it is boiled down
Into the yolks, before any butter
Into the butter, before it is mounted
questions.why: Each daughter is one addition to a finished béarnaise: tomato paste folded through for Choron, warm meat glaze whisked in for Foyot, both off the heat.

questions.q: Béarnaise is the classic French sauce for which food?
questions.answer: Grilled and roast beef
questions.why: Its vinegar and tarragon cut through the richness of beef, which is why it is the steak sauce; hollandaise and its lighter daughters lean to eggs, fish and asparagus.

questions.q: Compared with hollandaise, how thick is a béarnaise usually made?
questions.answer: A little thicker, to sit on meat
distractors: Much thinner, so it can be poured
Thin enough to soak into bread
questions.why: Béarnaise is spooned onto hot grilled meat, so a firmer body keeps it on the steak instead of pooling on the plate.

questions.q: Béarnaise is named for which place?
questions.answer: Béarn, home region of Henri IV
questions.why: The sauce honours Béarn, where Henri IV was born, whose name the Pavillon at Saint-Germain-en-Laye also carried.

questions.q: On which Brennan's plate is béarnaise printed as French béarnaise?
questions.answer: The breakfast and lunch hanger steak
distractors: The Redfish Véronique on the dinner menu
questions.why: Béarnaise is printed on the breakfast and lunch Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak; the dinner Creole Hanger Steak carries Madeira-glazed broccolini and chilli crisp, not béarnaise.

questions.q: Why might a béarnaise come out thin and slack?
questions.answer: The reduction was left too wet
distractors: Too much fresh tarragon went in
questions.why: A wet reduction carries extra water into the yolks, loosening the emulsion; boil it down until about 30 ml (2 tbsp) is left.

questions.q: A béarnaise tastes flat and buttery. What brings it back?
questions.answer: Vinegar drops and fresh tarragon
distractors: A pinch of sugar and some cream
Dried tarragon stirred in at the end
questions.why: Flatness means the reduction was timid; acid and fresh tarragon restore the edge, while dried tarragon lacks the fresh herb's lift.

entries.title: Marchand de vin
entries.summary: The wine merchant's sauce: red wine and shallot reduced into a brown sauce. New Orleans made its own glossy version of onion, garlic, often ham and mushroom, red wine and beef stock, and Brennan's serves it beneath the egg on the Eggs Hussarde.
entries.guest: Marchand de vin, the wine merchant's sauce, is a savoury, glossy red wine sauce, often with mushroom. On the Eggs Hussarde it sits beneath the egg, with hollandaise on top.

paras: Marchand de vin means wine merchant, and the sauce is named for what he sold: red wine, reduced with shallots and finished as a brown sauce. In France it is shallots cooked down in red wine with demi-glace (brown stock and brown sauce reduced until glossy), or a butter beaten with the same flavours and melted over a grilled steak. Either way it tastes of wine first and meat second.

New Orleans made its own version, and it is the one a Brennan's server needs. Onion and plenty of garlic stand in for some or all of the shallot, ham and mushrooms often join them, and red wine and beef stock are frequently bound with a roux into a glossy brown sauce, thicker and more savoury than the French reduction.

For the New Orleans style, melt 45 g (1.5 oz) of butter and cook a small onion, finely chopped, four cloves of garlic, 60 g (2 oz) of diced ham and 115 g (4 oz) of sliced mushrooms over moderate heat for 8 to 10 minutes, until soft and lightly browned. Stir in 30 g (1 oz) of flour and keep stirring for 5 to 8 minutes, until it smells nutty and turns light brown. That is a roux, flour cooked in fat, and it will thicken the sauce.

Pour in 250 ml (about 1 cup) of red wine and boil it down by half, which drives off the raw alcohol and concentrates the fruit. Add 500 ml (about 2 cups) of beef stock, a bay leaf and a sprig of thyme, and simmer gently for 20 to 30 minutes, skimming off any fat, until the sauce coats the back of a spoon. Season with salt, black pepper and a pinch of cayenne, and lift out the herbs.

The French sauce is quicker: reduce two finely chopped shallots in 250 ml (about 1 cup) of red wine by two thirds, add 250 ml (about 1 cup) of demi-glace, simmer for a few minutes, and finish off the heat with a knob of cold butter.

In the sauce tree, marchand de vin is a daughter of the brown family: a brown base, an aromatic and an acid reduction, here red wine. Its closest cousin is bordelaise, the French red wine sauce finished with beef marrow; bordelaise has its own entry, and in New Orleans its own meaning.

A raw, sharp taste of wine means the wine went in with the stock before it was reduced; reduce it by half first. A floury, pasty taste means the roux was not cooked long enough, or the sauce was not simmered after thickening; simmer it longer. A gluey, heavy sauce has too much roux or too much reduction; loosen it with hot stock. A greasy surface is fat from the ham and butter left in; draw the pan half off the heat so the fat gathers on one side, and skim it. A bitter sauce has burnt garlic or a scorched roux, which nothing hides: start again.

Classical French cooking used the wine merchant's flavours both as a sauce and as a butter for grilled steak. In New Orleans, Antoine's, open since 1840, is credited with making the sauce famous in the city. Eggs Hussarde, which Brennan's made famous from about 1950, put the sauce on the breakfast table, under poached eggs and beside hollandaise.

At the table, call it a savoury red wine and mushroom sauce, the house wording, once lineup has confirmed that tonight's carries mushroom; until then, a savoury red wine sauce. Never call it a bare red wine reduction, which undersells a sauce with real body. Whether it carries ham tonight, or what thickens it, is the chef's answer, not a guess. It is made with red wine, which matters to a guest who avoids alcohol; the kitchen confirms the rest.

At Brennan's, marchand de vin is the dark, winey half of the two sauces on the Eggs Hussarde and the Eggs Owen, beneath the egg with hollandaise above; on the Owen it echoes the short rib braised in red wine. New Orleans marchand de vin is often bound with a roux; whether ours is, and how dark that roux goes, is a question for the chef.

ratios.label: Flour to liquid, New Orleans style
ratios.value: 30 g (1 oz) of flour to 750 ml (about 3 cups) of wine and stock

ratios.label: Wine to stock
ratios.value: 1 part red wine to 2 parts beef stock, the wine reduced by half first

ratios.label: French style
ratios.value: 2 shallots and 250 ml (about 1 cup) red wine reduced by two thirds, then 250 ml (about 1 cup) demi-glace

faults.cause: The wine was not reduced before the stock went in.
faults.fix: Reduce the wine by half first; simmer a raw sauce longer.

faults.cause: The roux was undercooked, or the sauce was not simmered after thickening.
faults.fix: Simmer it gently for longer, stirring, until the raw flour taste goes.

faults.cause: Too much roux, or reduced too far.
faults.fix: Loosen it with hot stock, a little at a time, until it coats a spoon.

faults.cause: Fat from the ham and butter left unskimmed.
faults.fix: Set the pan half off the heat so the fat gathers on one side, and skim it.

faults.cause: Burnt garlic or a scorched roux.
faults.fix: Nothing hides it: start again, with gentler heat for the garlic and roux.

brennans.how: Beneath the poached eggs and coffee-cured Canadian bacon, with hollandaise on top. New Orleans marchand de vin is often bound with a roux; whether ours is, and how dark, is a question for the chef.

Under the soft-boiled egg with hollandaise, over red-wine-braised short rib débris and a Creole-spiced potato, the sauce echoes the braise. Whether tonight's carries ham or mushroom is a question for the chef.

cards.front: What does marchand de vin mean, and why the name?
cards.back: Wine merchant: the sauce is built on what he sold, red wine, reduced with shallot or onion into a brown sauce.

cards.front: What is marchand de vin in classical French cooking?
cards.back: Shallots reduced in red wine with demi-glace and finished with butter, or a butter beaten with the same flavours for a grilled steak.

cards.front: How does the New Orleans marchand de vin differ from the French?
cards.back: Onion and plenty of garlic, often ham and mushrooms, red wine and beef stock, frequently bound with a roux into a glossy brown sauce.

cards.front: What is a roux, and what does it do in marchand de vin?
cards.back: Flour cooked in fat until it smells nutty; it thickens the wine and stock into a glossy sauce that coats a spoon.

cards.front: Why is the red wine reduced before the stock goes in?
cards.back: Boiling it down by half drives off the raw alcohol and sharpness and concentrates the fruit; added unreduced, the wine tastes raw.

cards.front: Where does marchand de vin sit in the sauce tree?
cards.back: In the brown family, as a daughter built on a brown base; its closest cousin is bordelaise, which adds beef marrow.

cards.front: Which old New Orleans restaurant is credited with making marchand de vin famous in the city?
cards.back: Antoine's, open since 1840. Eggs Hussarde, made famous at Brennan's from about 1950, later put the sauce on the breakfast table.

cards.front: How should a server describe marchand de vin to a guest?
cards.back: As a savoury red wine and mushroom sauce, the house wording, once lineup confirms the mushroom; never as a bare red wine reduction, which undersells it.

cards.front: Which Brennan's dishes carry marchand de vin?
cards.back: The Eggs Hussarde and the Eggs Owen, beneath the egg, with hollandaise as the second sauce.

cards.front: A guest asks whether tonight's marchand de vin carries ham. What do you do?
cards.back: Ask the chef before promising: whether it carries ham or mushroom, and whether it is bound with a roux, are kitchen questions.

cards.front: A marchand de vin turns gluey and heavy. What happened, and what is the fix?
cards.back: Too much roux or too much reduction. Loosen it with hot stock, a little at a time, until it coats a spoon.

questions.q: What does the French name marchand de vin mean?
questions.answer: Wine merchant
questions.why: The sauce is named for the man who sold the wine; red wine is the flavour at its heart, French or New Orleans style.

questions.q: Which build describes a typical New Orleans marchand de vin?
questions.answer: Onion, garlic, ham, red wine, stock and roux
distractors: Egg yolk, butter, shallot, tarragon and vinegar
Milk, white roux, onion, clove and nutmeg
Tomato, the trinity, bay, thyme and cayenne
questions.why: New Orleans cooks built a glossy, roux-bound brown sauce on onion and garlic, often with ham and mushroom, red wine and beef stock.

questions.q: Why reduce the red wine by half before adding the stock?
questions.answer: To cook off its raw, sharp edge
distractors: To make the sauce paler in colour
To stop the roux from thickening
questions.why: Unreduced wine stays sharp and raw in the finished sauce; boiling it down first leaves its fruit and depth.

questions.q: Which sauce is marchand de vin's closest cousin in the brown family?
questions.answer: Bordelaise
questions.why: Both are red wine and shallot sauces on a brown base; bordelaise adds beef marrow, while béarnaise is an emulsion, Mornay white and provençale tomato.

questions.q: Which New Orleans restaurant, open since 1840, is credited with making marchand de vin famous in the city?
questions.answer: Antoine's
questions.why: Antoine's dates from 1840 and the house notes credit it with making the sauce famous; Galatoire's and Arnaud's opened in the twentieth century, and Commander's Palace later in the nineteenth.

questions.q: Which words describe marchand de vin to a Brennan's guest?
questions.answer: A savoury red wine and mushroom sauce
distractors: A sharp tarragon and shallot butter sauce
questions.why: That is the house wording; a bare reduction undersells a sauce with real body. Confirm tonight's ham or mushroom with the chef before you promise either.

questions.q: On the Eggs Hussarde, where does the marchand de vin sit?
questions.answer: Beneath the egg, with hollandaise on top
distractors: On the side, in a sauceboat
Over the hollandaise, brushed on as a glaze
Beside the egg, in a separate pool
questions.why: The Hussarde carries two sauces: the dark marchand de vin beneath the poached egg and the bright hollandaise above it.

questions.q: A guest asks whether tonight's marchand de vin has ham in it. What should a server do?
questions.answer: Check with the chef before promising
distractors: Say no, it is a plain wine reduction
Say yes, the recipe always has ham
questions.why: Whether tonight's sauce carries ham or mushroom is a question for the chef; a guess can mislead a guest.

questions.q: A marchand de vin has turned gluey and heavy. What is the fix?
questions.answer: Loosen it with hot stock, bit by bit
distractors: Boil it hard to tighten it further still
Add cold butter in one go
questions.why: Too much roux or reduction made it heavy; hot stock thins it back to a sauce that coats a spoon without dulling the flavour.
